newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Rifkind sees EU integration push danger.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rifkind sees EU integration push danger.

text.p: Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday Britain was "on balance hostile" to a single European currency and suggested democratic rights across the European Union could be trampled on in a rush to closer integration.
Rifkind told an audience in Bonn that proposals put forward by Germany for development of the bloc look to many people "like an agenda for creating a European state".

Rifkind's speech, the text of which was released in advance, was the second in a series he is delivering in EU capitals to set out Britain's case for a flexible EU of freely cooperating nation states.

By contrast, Germany is proposing more majority voting in key areas of decision making in Brussels, meaning member states could find themselves forced to implement regulations they had bitterly opposed.

Germany, impatient to consolidate the EU, is also the leading light in the drive to introduce a single European currency in 1999, and wants justice and home affairs issues to become part of Brussels' remit.
"It is no good saying that the convoy must not go at the pace of its slowest ship. We are not talking about convoys, we are talking about democracy," Rifkind said.
"The European Union cannot afford to brush aside the deeply-held concerns of its peoples just because they happen to be in a minority."

Listing proposals for closer integration which Bonn has put forward at the EU's Intergovernmental Conference, Rifkind said: "All of these proposals seem to point the same way -- a transfer of power from the member states to European institutions."
"At the least this looks like further centralisation. To many people it looks like an agenda for creating a European state."
He said ordinary people did not feel themselves part of a European nation and therefore were not willing to bow to the will of the majority in the EU.

"Why do people accept being overruled in national parliaments but not at the level of the European Union?" he asked. "Because while they feel part of a European culture, they do not feel themselves to be part of a single European nation."
